author: @horridohobbies
text:
Most iPhone users are casual users. They don't play demanding video games. They aren't serious photographers. They don't care about high refresh. Their phone easily lasts a day on a single charge because they don't spend hours and hours on their device.

For them, the iPhone 16 is an incremental upgrade of little significance (as have been the last several iPhone generations).

If you as a casual user are happy with your iPhone 12, 13, 14, or 15, you can easily skip the 16.

The new buttons are unimportant. The Camera Control button, in particular, is useless. It's superfluous and unnecessary. It's too fiddly and awkward to use. And it actually slows down your picture-taking task! 👎

Apple Intelligence isn't ready for prime time. And when it is ready, it won't be a big deal for most users. AI is more gimmicky than utilitarian.

About the only thing that impresses me is the ultrawide autofocus for better macro shots. But this is such a minor thing.

author: @Alphatech-e7d
text:
आपको iPhone से क्यों बचना चाहिए, समझदारी से काम लें, मेहनत की कमाई बर्बाद न करें !

Design and Display*
1. *Large notch*: The iPhone's notch can be obtrusive, especially when watching videos or gaming.
2. *Limited customization options*: iPhone's design and interface can feel restrictive for users who want more personalization.
3. *No headphone jack*: iPhone no longer has a headphone jack, which may inconvenience some users.

*Performance and Battery*
1. *60Hz refresh rate*: Even the latest iPhone models have a 60Hz refresh rate, which may seem outdated compared to Android devices with higher refresh rates.
2. *Battery life*: iPhone batteries can drain quickly, especially with heavy usage.
3. *No expandable storage*: iPhone doesn't have a microSD card slot, limiting storage expansion options.

*Camera*
1. *No optical zoom on lower models*: Lower-end iPhone models lack optical zoom, which can limit camera capabilities.
2. *No 8K video recording*: iPhone currently doesn't support 8K video recording.

*Software and Ecosystem*
1. *Closed ecosystem*: iPhone's closed system can make it difficult to transfer data or switch to a different platform.
2. *Limited multitasking*: iPhone's multitasking capabilities are limited compared to some Android devices.
3. *No customization options for default apps*: iPhone users are stuck with default apps for certain tasks.

*Price and Value*
1. *Expensive*: iPhones tend to be pricier than many Android devices with similar features.
2. *No affordable options*: The cheapest iPhone options are often older models or have limited storage.
3. *Additional costs for accessories*: iPhone users may need to purchase separate accessories, like headphones or a charging adapter.

*Other*
1. *No reverse wireless charging*: iPhone doesn't support reverse wireless charging, which can be convenient for charging other devices.
2. *Limited compatibility with non-Apple devices*: iPhone's closed ecosystem can make it difficult to integrate with non-Apple devices.
3. *Environmental concerns*: The frequent release of new iPhone models can contribute to electronic waste.

author: @aaditya57
text:
Bro battery degradation is more about user habits than brand name. 📱🔋

Charge cycles, heat, fast charging abuse — that's what kills batteries, not "Apple vs Android" debates. 😂

Modern iPhones (from iPhone 12 onwards) hold battery health extremely well if you charge smartly. 🔥

OnePlus 13 with 80W/100W charging will also lose capacity fast if you hammer it daily. Heat = degradation everywhere.

Also, if someone needs true battery life from iPhones → Pro Max and Plus models dominate easily.
(And good luck repairing OnePlus phones cheaply after 3–4 years 😂 — even Android repairs are getting costlier now.)

Buy what suits you — but facts are stronger than feelings. 😎

text: هناك العديد من الهواتف الذكية المميزة في السوق حاليًا.  تقدم كل شركة تقنيات متطورة ومزايا تنافسية.  يهتم المستخدمون بالبحث عن أفضل المواصفات والخصائص التي تناسب احتياجاتهم.  من المهم مقارنة المواصفات بدقة قبل اتخاذ قرار الشراء.  يجب مراعاة جوانب مثل الكاميرا والأداء وسعة البطارية.  الاختيار الأمثل يعتمد على تفضيلات المستخدم الفردية.  يُنصح بقراءة المراجعات ومشاهدة مقاطع الفيديو لمقارنة الأجهزة بشكل شامل.  في النهاية  الهدف هو الحصول على هاتف ذكي يلبي احتياجات المستخدم بأفضل طريقة.

text:
@Sacto1654 Not much, actually. There's a misconception that 120Hz runs all the time, but that's not true. It only kicks in while scrolling, in games that need it, or in other areas where smoothness is required. When you watch a video or perform other tasks, it automatically adjusts to 60Hz or whatever framerate is needed to play the content. So, the percentage of time 120Hz is active is minimal, but it makes a huge difference in day-to-day use. That's also why the impact on battery life is minimal, though smartphones today require daily charging anyway.

My point is that this feature has become standard and shouldn’t be overlooked by a company like Apple. Rumors suggest Apple will bring 120Hz to all iPhones next year, and I’m sure everyone will suddenly notice the real difference it makes.

author: @scr34m36
text:
Well, there's a lot of people talking about 60hz. Well here's my take on it:
Lately, I’ve found myself actually preferring 60Hz on the iPhone. Now, hear me out before hating on me.

I use both Android and iOS daily. My Android device runs on a Snapdragon 888, rocking a 120Hz AMOLED display, while my other go-to is the iPhone 15 Plus. On my Android, I’ve tweaked things like window animation, transition, and animator duration to 0.5x, while keeping the display locked at 120Hz refresh rate, which makes everything feel snappier and reduces input lag.

On the iPhone, though, I don’t have that kind of control because, well, iOS is locked down. But here’s what surprised me: the iPhone’s carefully tuned animations make its 60Hz feel just as smooth as 120Hz on Android, specifically the animation duration. And the bonus? It’s the reason my iPhone easily lasts 2+ days on moderate use, even with a charging cap of 80%.

Yet, Android remains my favorite because it lets me mold the experience how I want it. The openness of Android isn’t just a feature; it’s a whole vibe. Honestly, it’s the best mobile OS out there, no contest.

For me it’s like living with two personas: iPhone for the serious, task-driven side of me, and Android for everything else. Sure, there’s a list of things I prefer on Android, but iPhone does shine in certain areas too.

If Apple deserves backlash, it’s not for sticking with 60Hz displays but for their walled-garden approach, which doesn't let you actually "own" the device. They lock out the open-source community, barring the potential for innovation.

In the end, my dream device? Apple’s hardware, running Google’s Android. That would be the perfect fusion.
